Fat people on Airplanes

By: Michael Duffett | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Do I have a right to comfort in economy class on an airplane flight?

Summary:
It's an issue that won't go away. The comfort, or lack of comfort in economy classes of all airliners around the world. And when you have extra long legs or a very large built person is sitting next to you and the plane is full, with no opportunity to move to other seats, you could be destined for a 2-10 hour flight in discomfort. Part of the issue is that the seats are so narrow and that is because the airliners want to have as many passengers as possible to create revenue. They will of course argue that it is a way to keep the price down. Recently an italian lawyer sued Emirates because he was seated next to a very large man who overflowed into his personal space. There have been instances in the USA whereby huge people have actually been escorted off an airplane, as horrific as this sounds. This insert looks at the policies regarding very large people and flying. We know in South Africa that very large people are permitted to buy two seats to accommodate their size. But a question needs to be asked. Should airliners not accommodate very large people by having a few seats which are larger seats available to them. Is this not a humane answer to very overweight people? People can be very unkind about very large people. Sometimes they are so prejudiced against them they wont even strike up a conversation in an airplane. We speak to large people for their opinion and we do ask the airlines to what extent do they guarantee our comfort?

Press Release:


Mile High Comfort
Should our total weight – passenger and luggage – be taken into account at check-in when we board a flight? Recently, a disgruntled passenger sued an airline for a very uncomfortable nine-hour flight alongside an obese passenger. Carte Blanche asks: How should airlines cater for the needs of very large passengers?


Script:


Expect to fork out at lease R120 000 for a first class return ticket overseas. A business class return ticket aboard a south African airways airliner to Heathrow and back this month will cost close to R50 000.

Link: But for the rest of us who can't afford such luxuries its to the back of the plane in the cheap seats, economy class.

VOX POPS
Claire: Can you fit in comfortably?
Passenger at airport: Not at all, not at all. But look I’m 2 meters tall so...
Passenger at airport: You can do with more space actually.
Passenger at airport: No there’s not enough leg room and the seats are very very narrow.

Spare a thought for springbok legend, motivational speaker and super sport commentator Kobus Wiese.

Kobus: When you fly on smaller airlines and they don’t have business class seats its like when you enter, you sort of inhale deeply, really deeply and then you out hale when you land on the other side and get out of the door, that’s sort of how you fit into those seats.

Kobus often feels sorry for the passenger sitting next to him.

Kobus: I do, I get this responsibility attack and all of a sudden I try "oh I’m sorry mam, I'm sorry sir." You know but yah...

When a plane is choc a block, most of us can bear a short hop in economy class but it’s those long trips that seem to go on for an eternity.

LINK: You're on a long haul flight and you can tell its going to be packed. You say a silent prayer that the crying baby sits as far away from you as possible or at least there is an empty seat next to you, or a good looking stranger.

But if that stranger is going to be a person of considerable size, you may be in for an unconfutable ride. Aviation expert Linden Birns reminds us that when air travel was regulated in 1945, 90 kilograms was calculated as the average weight of an adult passenger.

Linden: Today there is consensus that actually we are all a bit larger and the average now is 100kg for the average adult.

But with obesity on the increase, economy class seats have not expanded with our waste lines, it seems!

LINK: Recently passenger comfort came into the spot light when an Italian lawyer sued emirates airlines because he felt his flight experience was compromised.

In July this year Italian attorney Giorgio Destro flew from Cape town to Dubai aboard an Emirates airliner. Seated next to him was a very large man whom he says spilt over into his space. He asked to be moved but the plane was full. he spent very little time in his seat.

Giorgio: About one or two hours. About two hours in a nine-hour flight.

He says he spent most of the flight standing or sitting a crew seat.

Giorgio: This man he was very worried. He said sorry for me. I feel sorry but I cannot do nothing.

Destro is suing Emirates for about R42 000 comprising ticket refunds and damages. The case is due to be heard in January in Padua Italy.
Emirates is unable to comment as its an ongoing legal matter.

Different legal systems exist around the word. Aviation Attorney Heather Manson believes that he he may have had difficulties in a south African court.

Heather: So south Africa currently doesn’t have any statuary right of a passenger to bring a claim against an airline as a result of discomfort

This surely is news to most of us.

Claire: What do the terms and conditions say on our tickets?
Heather: Airlines are all obliged to issue tickets to their passengers and there is certain information that that ticket needs to contain and that information is very factual. There is nothing that is specified in our tickets in relation to guarantees for comfort or anything like that.

Linden: Most of the compensation is to do with delayed flights or cancelled flights or if you bumped off a flight because they have over booked the flight or oversold it.

But it terms of passenger comfort there seem to be more complaints. Surely one of the worst was way back in 2002 when a uk woman was pinned down into her seat by the 146-kilogram female passenger next to her. Media reports said that she remained bedridden for a month after her ordeal, having suffered a blood clot in her chest, torn leg muscles and acute sciatica. In the end Virgin Atlantic paid her out 13000 pounds in compensation.

Linden: I think in most cases when it comes to consumer service orientated businesses the service provider is more inclined to settle and reach an agreement and satisfy their customer rather than have somebody go off and be grumpy and spread the word that this airline is uncaring. Airlines like anybody else care about their reputations especially in todays world where you have social media which is all about a discourse and the sharing of information and opinions.

South African airways spokesperson Tlali Tlali said that the airline encouraged people of size to contact then before a flight.

Tlali Tlali: They need to take steps in order to alert us as an airline about their situation on the basis of which we will be able to advise them as to what options they have available to them.

These options include flying during an off peak period, purchasing a second seat to ensure comfort- especially if the flight is full - and upgrading to business class.

Kobus normally travels business class but if that is unavailable, his agent books him two economy seats. He does however sometimes find himself in a single seat; he finds fellow south African passengers pretty accommodating.

Claire: Have you had any awkward situations? Has anyone ever complained that you were sitting next to them?
Kobus: Not really, I think we sort of, in that regard, people are quite tolerant you know, well in South Africa and sometimes also I have always found start chatting, have a laugh or two, a chuckle or two and you forget about the seat after a while.
Claire: Ah okay break the ice?
Kobus: that’s it!

LINK: An airlines configuration depends on two factors. The route that it is taking and the market that it serves. But what about configurations that are designed specifically for a particular population size?

And that was the focus of an honors student Zandile Hoyi’s thesis which looked at aircraft seats - which are generally designed for a western population.

Zandile: We got the south African population to sit on the seat to see whether or not they can sit comfortably as well as see if their anthropometric measures would be fitting to the seat.

Her test sample was 200 grahams town town residents

Zandile: We found that 40% of the female population actually required extra bum space and about 8% of the male population required this extra space as well.

And even more woes for people of size, if what Samoa airlines is doing, catches on. They seem to be the first airline in the world who are controversially charging passengers according to their weight.

SAA has no plans at this stage to follow suit, but it it was to become a norm, it would certainly hit the pockets of people like Kobus.

Kobus: So flying days are over for me because the excess baggage I’m going to pay is going to be like, its going to bankrupt me.

No doubt airlines all around the world will be watching the outcome of the matter between Giorgio Destro and Emirates airlines. If a court does make a ruling, it should have repercussions for both passengers and airline policies.

Heather: when putting together a policy, they need to ensure that it is a balance between their respective passenger rights. You've got to take into account the right against unfair discrimination as well as taking into account the consumers right in relation to the product they purchasing
